title: The Acts of Sharbil
author: The archives of Edessa
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 8
description: The chief priest of Edessa, who had led the city's sacrifices, becomes a Christian and is tried by the governor who had been his friend. From the Syriac records of that city, where the Church took root early and kept its own memory in its own tongue.

title: The Akathist Hymn to the Most Holy Theotokos (Russian)
author: Anonymous, of the sixth century
source: Received Russian text of the Orthodox Church
description: Sung standing, which is what its name says, on the Fridays of the Great Fast and whole on the Saturday of the fifth week. Twenty-four stanzas whose first letters run through the Greek alphabet, and a hundred and forty-four salutations beginning Hail, each one addressed to the Mother of God. It is of the sixth century; the Church has long named Romanos the Melodist among those who may have written it, and does not say so certainly.

title: Select Demonstrations
author: Aphrahat the Persian Sage
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 13
description: Written in the Persian empire while Shapur's persecution was falling on the Church there, and the earliest Syriac prose the Church has whole. Aphrahat answers an inquirer point by point on faith, on the monastic life, on the resurrection, on the office of a pastor, on Christ the Son of God, and on persecution and death, arguing throughout from Scripture and from the practice of his own churches and citing no philosopher at all. This edition prints eight of the twenty-three Demonstrations, keeping their numbers in the whole series, together with the letter that prompted them.
caution: Aphrahat is not given the title of a saint here. The Orthodox Church commemorates a Persian named Aphraates on the twenty-ninth of January, and he is another man: the hermit of Antioch whom Theodoret met as a boy and who died some sixty years after the Sage. The two are constantly taken for one. Nothing Aphrahat wrote was ever censured, and no council names him; he wrote a century before Ephesus, in a church that had not yet been divided by the controversies the Greek world was about to have. His eighth Demonstration teaches that the soul sleeps in the grave until the resurrection, which is not what the Church holds, and what she holds is said in her own prayers for the departed.

title: The Letters
author: St Basil the Great
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 8
description: Twenty years of a bishop's correspondence: consolation to the bereaved, rebuke to the powerful, instruction to his clergy, and the canonical letters to Amphilochius that the Church later received as canon law. Among them are the letters written while the Arian party held the East and Basil held Caesarea almost alone. This edition carries 325 of the 366 letters it numbers; most of those it does not print fall among the ones it marks as of doubtful authorship.
saint: Saint Basil the Great, Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia

title: The Canons of the Councils
author: The Councils of the Church
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 14
description: The canon law of the Church: the Apostolic Canons, the canons of the seven Ecumenical Councils and of the local councils received with them, the African Code, and the canonical epistles of the Fathers. Each conciliar canon carries its ancient epitome.

title: The Conferences
author: St John Cassian
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 11
description: Twenty-four conversations with the fathers of the Egyptian desert on prayer, discernment, purity of heart, and the goal of the monastic life.

title: The Institutes
author: St John Cassian
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 11
description: The customs of the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine, and the remedies for the eight principal faults, brought west by a disciple of the desert.

title: Commentary on Galatians
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Not homilies but a continuous commentary, the only one of its kind to survive from him, following the letter chapter by chapter through the quarrel over the law and the freedom for which Christ has set us free.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on First Corinthians
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 12
description: Forty-four homilies on the letter written to a church divided against itself, opened for a congregation that knew the same divisions. The chapters on the Eucharist, on love, and on the resurrection of the body are among the most quoted of all his preaching. The Argument stands first, as the edition prints it.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on First Thessalonians
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Eleven homilies on the earliest of the Apostle's letters, on the dead who sleep in Christ and the day that comes as a thief, and on the quiet labour asked of those who wait for it.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on First Timothy
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Eighteen homilies on the ordering of the Church: what is asked of a bishop, of a deacon, of a widow, and of the rich. The Argument stands first, as the edition prints it.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Second Corinthians
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 12
description: Thirty homilies on the most personal of the Apostle's letters, in which Paul defends his own ministry and boasts only of his weakness. Chrysostom, who would himself be driven from his see twice, reads it as a bishop reading a bishop.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Second Thessalonians
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Five homilies on the letter written to a church shaken by the report that the day of the Lord had already come, and on the man of sin who must be revealed before it does.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Second Timothy
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Ten homilies on the last letter the Apostle wrote, from a second imprisonment and in view of his death, charging a young bishop to keep what was entrusted to him.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles
author: St John Chrysostom
translator: J. Walker, J. Sheppard and H. Browne, revised by George B. Stevens
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 11
description: Fifty-five homilies preached at Constantinople on the acts of the Apostles, and the only commentary on that book to come down whole from the early Church in Greek. Chrysostom takes the young Church house by house and city by city, and turns almost every chapter to the manner of life it asks of those who read it.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Colossians
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Twelve homilies on the fulness of Christ, in whom all things hold together, preached against a piety that would put angels and observances between God and man.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Ephesians
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Twenty-four homilies on the letter of the one Body and the one Head, carrying his long treatment of marriage as the image of Christ and the Church, and of the armour of God. The Argument stands first, as the edition prints it.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 14
description: Thirty-four homilies on the priesthood of Christ and the new covenant.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on the Gospel of John
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 14
description: Eighty-eight homilies on the fourth Gospel, treating the Word made flesh and the discourses of the Lord.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 10
description: Ninety homilies expounding Matthew verse by verse, the fullest patristic commentary on the first Gospel.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Philemon
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Three homilies on the shortest of the Apostle's letters, sent back with a runaway slave. Chrysostom opens by answering those who thought so small a letter unworthy of Scripture. The Argument stands first, as the edition prints it.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Philippians
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Fifteen homilies on the letter of joy written from a prison, including the hymn of Christ's self-emptying, which Chrysostom expounds against those who would make the Son less than the Father. The Argument stands first, as the edition prints it.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Romans
author: St John Chrysostom
translator: J. B. Morris and W. H. Simcox
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 11
description: Thirty-two homilies on grace, law, and life in the Spirit.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on Titus
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 13
description: Six homilies on the letter to a bishop left in Crete to set in order what remained, and on the grace that teaches men to live soberly in the present age.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

title: Homilies on the Statues
author: St John Chrysostom
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 1, Vol. 9
description: Twenty-one homilies preached at Antioch during the crisis following the overturning of the imperial statues, on repentance, providence, and the fear of God.
saint: Repose of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople

source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
title: Κλήμεντος πρὸς Κορινθίους Α
author: St Clement of Rome
description: The Greek of Clement's letter to the Corinthians as Lake printed it, in the sixty-five chapters the Bryennios manuscript supplies.

title: The Instructor (Paedagogus)
author: Clement of Alexandria
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 2
description: Christ as the teacher who forms the Christian life, treating conduct, food, dress, speech, and the ordinary business of living.
caution: The Orthodox Church does not commemorate Clement of Alexandria, and he is not given the title of a saint here. The censure of Photius fell on his Hypotyposes, a book now lost and not among those kept here; of the Instructor he wrote favourably. Read as a witness to the Alexandria of about the year 200, not as a rule of faith.

title: The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians
author: St Clement of Rome
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 9
description: A letter from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth, which had deposed its presbyters. It appeals to the order the apostles left, names the succession by which bishops and deacons are appointed, and closes with a long prayer for rulers and for the whole world that is the earliest Christian liturgical prayer written down outside the Scriptures.

title: The Stromata, or Miscellanies
author: Clement of Alexandria
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 2
description: Miscellaneous studies weaving scripture and Greek learning toward the true gnosis of the Christian.
caution: The Orthodox Church does not commemorate Clement of Alexandria, and he is not given the title of a saint here. The censure of Photius fell on his Hypotyposes, a book now lost and not among those kept here. The Stromateis reasons freely with Greek philosophy and was never a rule of faith; read it as the exploration it is.

title: On the Dress of Virgins
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: To the women of Carthage who had vowed virginity, on modesty, wealth and display. One of the earliest witnesses to consecrated virginity as a settled state of life in the Church, a century before the monasteries.

title: On Jealousy and Envy
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: On the passion Cyprian says opened the first grave, since it was by the devil's envy that death entered the world, and on how it works inside a congregation.

title: On the Lord's Prayer
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: A commentary on the Our Father, petition by petition, and the earliest one the Church has. Cyprian's point throughout is that the prayer is said in the plural: we do not say my Father but our Father, because prayer for a Christian is never a private transaction.

title: On the Mortality
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: Written during the plague that emptied Carthage, to a people asking why Christians were dying with everyone else. Cyprian answers that the plague does not distinguish because it is not meant to, and that what it tests is whether a man believes what he says at the grave.

title: On the Advantage of Patience
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: That patience is not the temper of a man who does not mind, but a virtue learned from God, who bears with the world daily and makes His sun rise on the ungrateful.

title: On the Lapsed
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: Written when the persecution lifted and the Christians who had sacrificed to the idols came back asking to be received. The earliest treatment of a question the Church has faced in every generation since: what is done for a baptized man who has fallen, and on what terms he returns.

title: To Demetrian
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: An answer to a pagan who blamed the Christians for the plagues, the wars and the failing harvests, which is the oldest accusation there is. Cyprian replies that the world is growing old, and that the man who blames the Christians has not asked what he himself owes.

title: On the Unity of the Church
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: Written when a schism had opened at Rome and another threatened at Carthage, and the earliest sustained argument that the Church is one thing and not many: that her unity is not an achievement to be worked towards but a fact to be kept, and that the man who leaves her leaves what he was seeking.

title: On the Vanity of Idols
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: That the gods of the nations were men, that the demons took their names, and that the God the Christians worship is the one who made what the others are carved from.

title: On Works and Alms
author: St Cyprian of Carthage
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: On almsgiving, and on the sins committed after baptism that a Christian supposes he can do nothing about. Cyprian's answer is that mercy shown is the remedy the Lord Himself named, and that the man who keeps his money keeps his wound.

title: The Didache
author: The Twelve Apostles
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 7
description: The earliest surviving manual of Christian practice, covering the two ways, baptism, fasting, the Eucharist, the discernment of prophets, and the Lord's coming.
saint: Synaxis of the Holy, Glorious and All-Praised Twelve Apostles

title: Διδαχὴ τῶν δώδεκα ἀποστόλων
author: The Twelve Apostles
source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
description: The Greek of the Didache as Kirsopp Lake printed it, from the manuscript Philotheos Bryennios found at Constantinople in 1873, which is the only complete copy the Church has.
saint: Synaxis of the Holy, Glorious and All-Praised Twelve Apostles

author: Dionysius the Areopagite
source: The Works of Dionysius the Areopagite
publisher: James Parker and Co., London and Oxford
title: On Divine Names
description: On what may be said of God from the names Scripture gives Him: Good, Being, Life, Wisdom, Power, Peace. The argument throughout is that every name is given from what God does rather than from what He is, and that He remains beyond all of them.
caution: These writings were transmitted under the name of the Dionysius whom the Apostle Paul converted at Athens, and they are not his: they show a liturgy and a vocabulary of about the year 500. The Church received the writings and read them as her own, and St Maximus the Confessor wrote on them; she never received a claim about whose hand held the pen. They are kept under the name the manuscripts carry, and the date given is the date they were written.

author: Dionysius the Areopagite
source: The Works of Dionysius the Areopagite
publisher: James Parker and Co., London and Oxford
title: Ecclesiastical Hierarchy
description: On the visible order of the Church as the earthly answer to the heavenly one: baptism, the synaxis, the chrism, the ordinations, the monastic tonsure, and the burial of the dead, each treated as a rite and then as what the rite means.
caution: These writings were transmitted under the name of the Dionysius whom the Apostle Paul converted at Athens, and they are not his: they show a liturgy and a vocabulary of about the year 500. The Church received the writings and read them as her own, and St Maximus the Confessor wrote on them; she never received a claim about whose hand held the pen. They are kept under the name the manuscripts carry, and the date given is the date they were written.

author: Dionysius the Areopagite
source: The Works of Dionysius the Areopagite
publisher: James Parker and Co., London and Oxford
title: On the Heavenly Hierarchy
description: On the ranks of the angels and how each order receives light and passes it on. This is where the familiar ordering comes from, seraphim and cherubim and thrones down to the angels who are sent to men, and the principle that God works through an order rather than around it.
caution: These writings were transmitted under the name of the Dionysius whom the Apostle Paul converted at Athens, and they are not his: they show a liturgy and a vocabulary of about the year 500. The Church received the writings and read them as her own, and St Maximus the Confessor wrote on them; she never received a claim about whose hand held the pen. They are kept under the name the manuscripts carry, and the date given is the date they were written.

author: Dionysius the Areopagite
source: The Works of Dionysius the Areopagite
publisher: James Parker and Co., London and Oxford
title: Letters
description: Eleven letters as this edition prints them, from a note of a few lines to a treatise on the divine judgment. The seventh answers a philosopher who had attacked the Christians; the eighth rebukes a monk who had refused communion to a penitent.
caution: These writings were transmitted under the name of the Dionysius whom the Apostle Paul converted at Athens, and they are not his: they show a liturgy and a vocabulary of about the year 500. The Church received the writings and read them as her own, and St Maximus the Confessor wrote on them; she never received a claim about whose hand held the pen. They are kept under the name the manuscripts carry, and the date given is the date they were written.

author: Dionysius the Areopagite
source: The Works of Dionysius the Areopagite
publisher: James Parker and Co., London and Oxford
title: Mystic Theology
description: Five short chapters, and the root of the apophatic tradition of the East: that God is known by putting away what He is not, that the affirmations fail before the denials do, and that at the last even the denials must be let go.
caution: These writings were transmitted under the name of the Dionysius whom the Apostle Paul converted at Athens, and they are not his: they show a liturgy and a vocabulary of about the year 500. The Church received the writings and read them as her own, and St Maximus the Confessor wrote on them; she never received a claim about whose hand held the pen. They are kept under the name the manuscripts carry, and the date given is the date they were written.

author: St Ephraim the Syrian
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 13
title: Fifteen Hymns For the Feast of the Epiphany
description: Hymns for the Theophany, on the Jordan, on the descent into the water, and on what baptism does to the one baptized. The thirteenth is headed the Hymn of the Baptized and is sung in their own voice.

author: St Ephraim the Syrian
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 13
title: Three Homilies
description: Three homilies: on our Lord, on admonition and repentance, and on the sinful woman who anointed His feet. The last is a dialogue, and the seller of ointment is given lines.

author: St Ephraim the Syrian
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 13
title: Nineteen Hymns on the Nativity of Christ in the Flesh
translator: J. B. Morris and A. Edward Johnston
description: Hymns for the Feast of the Nativity, on the God who was carried by the one He carries, and on what it is for the Ancient of Days to be an infant. The eleventh is given wholly to the Virgin Mother speaking to her Child.

author: St Ephraim the Syrian
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 13
title: The Nisibene Hymns
translator: J. T. Sarsfield Stopford, revised by John Gwynn
description: Hymns written while Nisibis was under siege by the Persians and after its surrender drove Ephraim into exile at Edessa. They move between the city's walls and the soul's; a set in the middle honors the three bishops who held the city, and the long closing sequence is an argument with Death and Satan, who are given speeches of their own and answer back. This edition carries forty-five of the seventy-seven hymns, printing them in the numbering of the whole series so the gaps are visible, and it marks each gap where it falls: two of the pieces here are the editor's own brackets recording which hymns are wanting, which survives only as a fragment, and which concern Edessa.

author: St Ephraim the Syrian
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 13
title: The Pearl. Seven Hymns on the Faith
translator: J. B. Morris and A. Edward Johnston
description: Seven short hymns on faith, turning on a pearl Ephraim says he took up and questioned, and which answered him about the Son.

source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
title: Βαρνάβα ἐπιστολή
author: St Barnabas the Apostle
description: The Greek of the letter transmitted under the name of Barnabas.

source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
title: Πρὸς Διόγνητον
author: Mathetes
description: The Greek of the letter to Diognetus.

title: Church History
author: Eusebius of Caesarea
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 1
description: The first history of the Church, from the apostles to the peace of Constantine, preserving many documents and martyr accounts otherwise lost.
caution: Eusebius was provisionally excommunicated at Antioch in 325 for Arian sympathies and cleared at Nicaea the same year, and the Seventh Ecumenical Council named him an Arian. He is read here as the Church's first historian, for the documents and the accounts of the martyrs that he alone preserved, and not as a teacher of doctrine.

title: The Book of Pastoral Rule
author: St Gregory the Dialogist
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 12
description: On the burden of the pastoral office and how a shepherd should teach each kind of soul differently.
saint: Saint Gregory Dialogus, Pope of Rome

title: On the Baptism of Christ
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: A sermon for the Theophany, on what is done in the water, and on why the Lord who needed no cleansing went down into it.

title: On the Holy Spirit, Against the Macedonians
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: Against those who confessed the Son and denied the Spirit, written in the years around the Council of Constantinople, which settled the question.

title: On the Holy Trinity
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: A letter to Eustathius on why confessing three persons is not confessing three Gods.

title: On Infants' Early Deaths
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: To Hierius, who had asked what becomes of children who die before they can choose anything. Gregory refuses the easy answers on both sides and reasons instead from what God is.

title: On the Making of Man
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: Written to finish what his brother Basil left at the sixth day of the Hexaemeron. On what it means that man was made in the image of God, on the union of soul and body, and on the resurrection of the body, with a long look at how the body is built.

title: Funeral Oration on Meletius
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: Preached at Constantinople over the bishop who had presided at the Council and died while it was sitting.

title: On "Not Three Gods"
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: To Ablabius, who had asked the obvious question: if Peter, James and John are three men, why are the Father, the Son and the Spirit not three Gods. The answer turns on what a nature is and what a person is.

title: On Pilgrimages
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: A letter arguing that going to Jerusalem is not itself a means of grace, and that a change of place is not a change of heart.

title: On the Faith
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: A short statement of the faith addressed to Simplicius.

title: On Virginity
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: Written for those considering the celibate life, and against the notion that it is a rejection of marriage. Gregory, who was himself married, argues that virginity is a way of loving God undivided, and that the man who despises marriage has misunderstood both.

title: On the Soul and the Resurrection
author: St Gregory of Nyssa
translator: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 5
description: A dialogue held at the deathbed of his sister Macrina, who does most of the arguing. On what the soul is, what becomes of it at death, what the resurrection of the body means, and why grief is not a reason to doubt any of it.

title: Treatise on Christ and Antichrist
author: St Hippolytus of Rome
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: The earliest surviving Christian treatment of the last things as a subject in its own right, reading Daniel and the Apocalypse together. Hippolytus was a presbyter of Rome and a hearer of Irenaeus, who had heard Polycarp, who had heard the Apostle John.
saint: Hieromartyr Hippolytus, and those with him

title: Fragments from the Scriptural Commentaries
author: St Hippolytus of Rome
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: What survives of Hippolytus reading the Scriptures: on the six days, on Genesis, on Kings, the Psalms, Proverbs, the Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, Matthew and Luke, and at length on Daniel, where the seventy weeks and the fourth kingdom are read as the Church has read them since. The edition prints the doubtful fragments separately and says so in its own headings.
saint: Hieromartyr Hippolytus, and those with him

source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
title: Ἰγνατίου ἐπιστολαί
author: St Ignatius of Antioch
description: The Greek of the seven letters Ignatius wrote on the road to Rome, one unit to a letter as the English edition has them.
saint: Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bishop of Antioch

title: Against Heresies
author: St Irenaeus of Lyons
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 1
description: Written against the Gnostic teachers of the second century, and in the course of refuting them the earliest full account of what the Church holds and how she knows it: the faith received from the apostles, kept by the churches they founded, and traceable through the bishops they appointed. Irenaeus heard Polycarp, who had heard the Apostle John.

title: On the Holy Images
author: St John of Damascus
source: St John Damascene on Holy Images, followed by three sermons on the Dormition
description: Three apologies written while the images were being taken down by imperial order, and the defense on which the Seventh Ecumenical Council settled the question: that the invisible God, having become visible in the flesh, may be depicted in what He assumed; that the honor paid to the image passes to the one it represents; and that matter is not despised by the God who made it and was born into it. Parts I, II and III are the three apologies, each gathering the testimony of earlier Fathers behind it. The three sermons that follow are on the Dormition of the Theotokos; the translator gives them the Western title and sets the Greek beside it, and the Greek is koimesis, the falling asleep.

title: Dialogue with Trypho
author: St Justin the Philosopher
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 1
description: A sustained dialogue with a Jewish interlocutor on the law, the prophecies of Christ, and the calling of the nations.
saint: Martyr Justin the Philosopher and those with him at Rome

title: The Life and Passion of Cyprian
author: Pontius the Deacon
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 5
description: Written by the deacon who served him and went with him into exile, and the first Christian biography of a single man that survives. It ends with the sentence read out at Sextus, and what the bishop said when he heard it.

title: The Life of Saint Hilarion
author: St Jerome
translator: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 6
description: The man who carried the monastic life from Egypt into Palestine, having gone as a boy to see Antony in the desert and come back to a country that had no monks in it. Jerome wrote it from what the old men of Gaza still remembered.

title: The Life of Malchus, the Captive Monk
author: St Jerome
translator: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 6
description: A monk carried off by raiders into the Syrian desert and made a herdsman, told to Jerome by the old man himself. It is the shortest of his lives and the most nearly a tale, and he says at the outset that he writes it to try his hand before attempting a history of the Church.

title: The Life of Paulus the First Hermit
author: St Jerome
translator: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 6
description: The first of the desert solitaries, who went into the Thebaid in the persecution of Decius and stayed sixty years, and the visit Antony made to him at the end of it. Jerome wrote it as a young man, and it is the book that gave the West its picture of the desert.

title: On the Life of Saint Martin
author: Sulpitius Severus
source: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series 2, Vol. 11
description: The soldier who cut his cloak in two at the gate of Amiens, and afterwards bishop of Tours. Written by a man who knew him and published while he was still alive, which its author says plainly, and which is why it reads less like a memorial than a report.

title: The Prayers Proper to the Liturgy of St Basil the Great
author: St Basil the Great
source: Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic (Greco-Russian) Church
publisher: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, Boston and New York
description: The Liturgy of St Basil is the Liturgy the Church serves ten times in the year - on the Sundays of the Great Fast, on Holy Thursday and Holy Saturday, at the Nativity and the Theophany, and on his own feast - and it is the same service as the Liturgy of St John Chrysostom except in certain prayers the priest says secretly, one hymn, and three phrases in the consecration. Those are given here, in the order the service takes them, from an English service book of the Orthodox Church. The longest of them is the anaphora, which tells the whole history of salvation from the making of man to the second coming in one sentence after another, and which the Chrysostom shortens; the reader who wants to know why the Church keeps two liturgies will find the answer there.
saint: Saint Basil the Great, Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia

source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 7
title: The Divine Liturgy of James the Holy Apostle and Brother of the Lord
author: St James the Brother of the Lord
saint: Apostle James, the Brother of the Lord
description: The Liturgy of Jerusalem, served in the church where the Church herself began and kept to this day on the feast of St James. It is the fullest of the ancient rites and the one the Byzantine Liturgy grew from: the same Trisagion, the same kiss of peace, the same calling down of the Spirit upon the gifts, the same cry that the holy things are for the holy, in older and longer words. The great intercession names the Theotokos, the saints and the departed by name, and the prayers of the priest are given whole, including those he says under his breath.
caution: The Church has served this Liturgy in Jerusalem from antiquity and keeps it still on the feast of St James, and she has never taught that the Apostle wrote out the text that carries his name. It grew in the church he governed and is called by his, as a rite is called by the see that serves it. What St Cyril of Jerusalem describes to his catechumens in the fourth century is recognisably this service; the manuscripts that preserve it are later, and it is given here as they have it.

source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 7
title: The Divine Liturgy of the Holy Apostle and Evangelist Mark, The Disciple of the Holy Peter
author: St Mark the Evangelist
description: The Liturgy of Alexandria, the church St Mark founded, kept under his name as the rite of Jerusalem is kept under St James's. Its order is not the Byzantine one - the great intercession comes before the anaphora rather than within it, and the prayers for the rise of the Nile stand where a northern rite asks for seasonable weather - and it is the plainest evidence the shelf holds that the Church's worship was one thing said differently in different places.
caution: The rite of Alexandria, kept under the name of the Evangelist who founded that church, on the same footing as the Liturgy of St James is kept under his: the Church received the service, not a claim about whose hand wrote it down. It is not in use in the Orthodox Church today, and is here as the worship of Alexandria in the centuries when it was.

title: The Martyrdom of Barsamya
author: The archives of Edessa
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 8
description: The bishop of Edessa brought before the governor for having baptised Sharbil, and the argument that follows about who made the city's gods.

title: The Martyrdom of Habib the Deacon
author: The archives of Edessa
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 8
description: A deacon of Edessa under Licinius, who gave himself up rather than let his people be seized in his place, and the mother who followed him to the fire.

title: The Martyrdom of Ignatius
author: The Church of Antioch
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 1
description: The account of the road from Antioch to Rome and of what waited at the end of it, written by those who went with him. He had asked the Romans not to hinder the beasts, and this is the record of the day they were not hindered.

title: The Martyrdom of Justin and his Companions
author: The Roman court record
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 1
description: Not a narrative but the examination itself: the prefect Rusticus asking the questions and six Christians answering them, taken down as the court took it down. Justin had written two Apologies to emperors; this is what he said when no longer writing.

source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
title: Μαρτύριον τοῦ ἁγίου Πολυκάρπου
author: The Church of Smyrna
description: The Greek of the letter the church of Smyrna sent after Polycarp's death.

title: The Martyrdom of the Holy Confessors Shamuna, Guria and Habib
author: Theophilus of Edessa
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 8
description: The two confessors of Edessa under Diocletian, with the deacon Habib who followed them, whom that city has kept together in one commemoration ever since and to whose shrine the famous oath of the Gothic soldier was carried.

title: The Banquet of the Ten Virgins
author: St Methodius of Olympus
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 6
description: Ten virgins in a garden, each giving a discourse in praise of chastity, in deliberate imitation of Plato's Symposium and in answer to it. The earliest sustained Christian treatment of virginity, written by the bishop who was the first to answer Origen at length.

title: On First Principles (De Principiis)
author: Origen
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 4
description: The first systematic treatment of Christian doctrine, treating God, the rational creation, the world, free will, and Scripture.
caution: Origen is named among the condemned at the Fifth Ecumenical Council, and the speculations this book is best known for, the pre-existence of souls and a final restoration of all things, are among the teachings the Church rejected. It is kept here as a document of the third century and as the book the Church later answered, not as a statement of the faith. Read it knowing what she decided.

title: The Christians in Outside Eyes
author: Witnesses outside the Church
translator: William Stearns Davis (Pliny and Trajan); Alfred Church and William Brodribb (Tacitus); H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler (Lucian)
source: Readings in Ancient History, Vol. II; The Annals of Tacitus; The Works of Lucian of Samosata, Vol. IV
description: What men outside the Church wrote about the Christians in the first two centuries: a Roman governor reporting to his emperor on how they worshipped, a Roman historian on Nero's executions, and a Greek satirist on how they cared for their own. None of them believed; all of them were hostile; every one of them describes a thing that was there to be described.

title: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity
author: Perpetua of Carthage and an eyewitness
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 3
description: The oldest writing that survives from the hand of a Christian woman. Perpetua kept a diary in prison and set down her own visions and the argument with her father; another hand records what happened in the amphitheatre at Carthage, and the slave Felicity who gave birth in the prison days before.
saint: Martyrs Perpetua, a woman of Carthage, and the Catechumens: Saturus, Revocatus, Saturninus, Secundulus and Felicitas
caution: The Church honours these martyrs and has kept their day since the third century; Perpetua, Felicity and their companions stand in the calendar on the first of February. The text itself carries the marks of the Montanists, who claimed it: the framing preface speaks in their manner of new prophecy, and Tertullian, who had gone over to them, is often supposed to have edited it. What Perpetua wrote in prison is her own and is why the book is here. The frame around it is the reason the note is here.

source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
title: Πολυκάρπου πρὸς Φιλιππησίους
author: St Polycarp of Smyrna
description: The Greek of Polycarp's letter to the Philippians.

title: The Passion of the Scillitan Martyrs
author: The proconsular record
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 9
description: The earliest dated document of the Church in Africa and the earliest in Latin: a proconsul at Carthage in the year 180, twelve Christians from Scilli, and a hearing that runs a page and a half. Asked what is in their satchel, they answer, books and the letters of Paul, a just man.

title: An Ancient Homily
author: An unknown preacher
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 9
description: The earliest Christian sermon that survives: not a letter and not by Clement, but an address preached to a congregation and copied afterwards beside his, which is how it came to be called his second epistle. It opens by telling the hearers to think of Jesus Christ as of God, and of themselves as having been rescued from very little into very much.
caution: This homily was copied and read beside the letter of Clement of Rome and came to be called his second epistle. It is neither his nor a letter, and it is not among the canonical Scriptures. It is kept here as what it is, the oldest surviving sermon preached to a Christian congregation.

source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
title: Ὁμιλία ἀρχαία
author: An unknown preacher
description: The Greek of the oldest surviving Christian sermon, as Lake printed it.

title: The Shepherd of Hermas
author: St Hermas of the Seventy
source: Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 2
description: An early Roman apocalypse in three parts, the Visions, the Mandates, and the Similitudes, widely read in the ancient Church and treating repentance, the building of the tower which is the Church, and the commandments of the angel of repentance.
caution: The Shepherd was read aloud in some churches in the early centuries and is quoted by the Fathers, but it is not among the canonical Scriptures and was not received as such.

title: Ποιμὴν τοῦ Ἑρμᾶ
author: St Hermas of the Seventy
source: The Apostolic Fathers, Loeb Classical Library
description: The Shepherd as Lake printed it: five Visions, twelve Mandates and ten Similitudes, in the divisions the English edition here also keeps. The tenth Similitude is in Latin, which is how it survives; the Greek of the closing section is lost and the edition prints the old Latin version in its place.
